    How Kumquat teaches, and why

    Natural frequencies. Bayesian problems taught as “of 1000 people…” are solved by ~75–80% of medical students, versus ~20% with formulas. That’s the Tree drill, and it’s why p values are taught the same way.

    Predict, then learn. Lessons open with a myth check: you commit to an answer before the explanation, which makes the correction stick.

    Retrieval and spacing. You answer before you see; misses return after 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days. Confident misses come back first.

    Interleaving. Mixed drills make you pick the method from the problem, which is the exam skill.

    Generation. For calculations you type the number first; options appear only if you ask.

    Faded worked examples, teach-back, calibration. Scaffolding fades as you grow; you explain ideas in writing and compare with a model; you flag guesses.

    Hold anything (a number, a chip, a card) to get an explanation or more actions.

    Diagnostic tests

    Cut-off dial

    Two overlapping populations, one threshold. Where you draw the line decides who gets called sick. Step 1 labels the candidate cut-offs A to E.

    Move left → sens ↑, NPV ↑, spec ↓, PPV ↓. More false positives.

    Move right → spec ↑, PPV ↑, sens ↓, NPV ↓. More false negatives.

    Math foundations

    Math gym

    The three bits of maths that epidemiology leans on most: where a value sits on the normal curve, how odds relate to probability, and what skew does to averages.

    1 · The normal curve · SBP mean 120, SD 10

    Bands show ±1, ±2, ±3 SD: 68%, 95%, 99.7%. Tails beyond +1, +2, +3 SD: 16%, 2.5%, 0.15%.

    2 · Probability ↔ odds
    odds = p / (1 − p)
    p = odds / (1 + odds)

    Small probabilities: odds ≈ probability. That’s why OR ≈ RR for rare outcomes.

    3 · Skew

    Drill it

    Odds, z-scores, percentage points, herd immunity.

    Diagnostic tests

    Fagan nomogram

    Start with how likely the disease was before the test. The likelihood ratio tells you how far a result should move you.

    Post-test probability

    McGee’s shortcut (works for pre-test 10–90%): LR 2, 5, 10 add about 15, 30, 45 percentage points. LR 0.5, 0.2, 0.1 subtract the same.

    Inference & power

    Power playground

    The grey curve is the world where the treatment does nothing. The orange curve is the world where it works. Your study has to tell them apart.

    Significance level α

    Type I (α) · smoke alarm with no fire. You call an effect that isn’t there.

    Type II (β) · fire with no alarm. You miss an effect that is real.

    α · false alarm
    β · missed effect
    Power · caught it

    Inference & power

    CI dance

    True mean systolic BP in a workforce is 130 mmHg (SD 15). Each line is one study that samples n workers and builds a confidence interval. Count how often the truth gets caught.

    Confidence level
    Interval method

    Caught the truth
    –

    0 studies

    “95% confidence” describes the method: across many studies, 95% of intervals contain the true value. Any single interval either does or doesn’t.

    Bigger n → narrower intervals. Higher confidence → wider intervals.

    Study designs

    Study designs

    Each design answers a particular kind of question and yields its own measure of association. Know the measure and you know the design.

    Hierarchy of evidence (for treatment questions)
    The 3-second decoder

    Did the investigator assign the exposure? Yes → experimental (randomised? → RCT).

    No, observational. Start from exposure and follow forward → cohort (RR). Start from outcome and look back → case-control (OR). One snapshot → cross-sectional (prevalence). Groups, not people → ecological.

    Bias bestiary

    Choosing tests

    Test picker

    Two or three questions about your data and you have the test. Then practise until you skip the tree.

    The cheat line

    Normal & 2 groups → t-test (paired or independent). Not normal → Mann–Whitney or Wilcoxon. 3+ groups → ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis. Categories → χ² or Fisher; paired → McNemar. Time to event → log-rank, Cox. Agreement → kappa (categories), Bland–Altman or ICC (measurements).

    Critical appraisal

    Appraisal kit

    Three questions for every paper: Is it valid? What are the results? Will they help my patients? Use the checklist while you read.

    Tap any part of the plot

    Illustrative meta-analysis: workplace exercise programmes and sickness absence (odds ratios). Tap a square, a line, the diamond or the vertical line.

    GRADE in one minute

    How certain is the evidence?

    StartRCTs → High · Observational → Low
    Down ↓Risk of bias · Inconsistency (I²) · Indirectness · Imprecision (wide CI) · Publication bias
    Up ↑Large effect (RR > 2 or < 0.5) · Dose-response · All plausible confounding would reduce the effect
    ResultHigh · Moderate · Low · Very low — for the body of evidence on one outcome, not for one paper
    Appraisal drill

    ITT, I², funnel plots, forest plots, loss to follow-up. Ten questions.

    30-day programme

    Mastery month

    Thirty plan days. A day moves on only when its missions are done, so a missed day waits for you instead of being lost. Each session is sized to your daily time; what doesn’t fit spills to the next one. Missions tick themselves off; mock exams fall on plan days 15, 21, 28 and 30.

    Coverage

    Blueprint

    Every epidemiology and biostatistics item the Steps can ask. Rate each one honestly; the chip next to each topic shows your real accuracy over your last answers. Your ratings are a confidence check and never raise your mastery %: only answers do (a topic counts once you score 80%+ over your last 10 or more).

    Role-play

    Casebook

    Ten real outbreaks, trials and scandals that shaped epidemiology. You step into the story, make the calls the investigators faced, then see what really happened.

    Measuring disease

    Outbreak simulator

    A town of 10,000. Ten people arrive infected. Set how contagious the pathogen is and how many people are already immune, and watch the epidemic run.

    R₀ = contacts × chance × days

    R₀ = contacts per day × chance of transmission per contact × infectious days. Cut any one (distancing, masks, early isolation) and R₀ falls: the curve gets lower and smaller, not just slower.

    Herd immunity threshold = 1 − 1/R₀. Preset numbers are illustrative splits of each pathogen’s R₀.

    Susceptible
    Infected now
    Recovered / immune
    Herd immunity line
    Bias & confounding

    Confounding lab

    Build a confounder from scratch. 1000 exposed and 1000 unexposed people, a baseline outcome risk of 5%, and a third variable you control. Then stratify and see what’s really going on.

    Arrow thickness shows how strongly the confounder is tied to exposure (left) and outcome (right).

    Appraisal

    Funnel lab

    Forty trials of the same treatment. Big trials sit at the top, tightly around the truth; small ones scatter widely at the bottom. Now switch on publication bias and watch the small, disappointing trials vanish.

    Published trial
    Never published
    True effect
    Pooled estimate

    Set the true effect to 1.0 (the drug does nothing) and switch bias on. The small trials that found nothing, or harm, go unpublished, and the pooled published OR drifts below 1: a benefit that doesn’t exist. Big trials resist this, which is why the gap varies run to run. That’s why trials must be registered before they start.
